questions.stem: A 55‑year‑old man presents with a solitary, firm, non‑mobile mass in the right upper quadrant. Imaging shows a well‑defined lesion with central calcification. Which of the following is the most likely histological diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Focal nodular hyperplasia (FNH) is a benign hepatic lesion that typically presents as a well‑defined mass with a central stellate scar (calcification). Hepatocellular carcinoma and metastatic adenocarcinoma are malignant and usually lack a central scar. Hepatic adenoma is also benign but does not characteristically show a central scar.

questions.stem: A 45‑year‑old woman presents with a 2‑cm firm, non‑tender mass in the left breast. Core needle biopsy shows a proliferation of ductal epithelial cells forming irregular glandular structures with high mitotic activity and areas of necrosis. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The biopsy shows malignant ductal cells with necrosis and high mitotic rate, classic for invasive ductal carcinoma. Fibroadenoma and intraductal papilloma are benign and lack necrosis; phyllodes tumour shows a leaf‑like stromal pattern, not ductal epithelial proliferation.

questions.stem: A 58‑year‑old man presents with a 4‑cm ulcerated mass in the sigmoid colon. Histology shows a well‑differentiated adenocarcinoma with a desmoplastic stromal reaction and lymphovascular invasion. Which of the following is the most likely histological grade of this tumour?
questions.explanation: The tumour is well‑differentiated but shows lymphovascular invasion and a desmoplastic reaction, indicating a moderate degree of cytologic atypia and mitotic activity – characteristic of Grade II. Grade I tumours are highly differentiated with minimal atypia; Grade III shows marked pleomorphism and high mitotic rate; Grade IV is undifferentiated.
questions.source: Tumour grading principles in colorectal carcinoma

questions.stem: A 58‑year‑old man presents with a 4‑cm exophytic mass on the left upper quadrant of the pancreas. Fine‑needle aspiration cytology shows cells with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm, prominent nucleoli, and a high mitotic rate. Immunohistochemistry is positive for chromogranin A and synaptophysin, but negative for cytokeratin 7. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The tumour shows neuroendocrine markers (chromogranin A, synaptophysin) and lacks cytokeratin 7, which is typical for pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours. Ductal adenocarcinoma would be cytokeratin positive and lack neuroendocrine markers; solid pseudopapillary neoplasms are usually CK7 positive and have characteristic pseudopapillary architecture; acinar cell carcinoma expresses trypsin and chymotrypsin, not neuroendocrine markers.

questions.stem: A 58‑year‑old man presents with a 3‑month history of painless jaundice and weight loss. Imaging shows a 4‑cm mass in the head of the pancreas with encasement of the superior mesenteric artery but no distant metastases. A fine‑needle aspiration biopsy reveals a malignant epithelial tumour with a high Ki‑67 index, nests of cells with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm, and prominent nucleoli. Which of the following immunohistochemical stains is most likely to confirm the diagnosis of a pancreatic neuroendocrine tumour?
questions.explanation: Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours characteristically express neuroendocrine markers such as chromogranin A and synaptophysin. CK7 is a cytokeratin seen in many adenocarcinomas, CDX2 is intestinal, and S100 is a neural crest marker. Therefore chromogranin A is the most specific confirmatory stain.
